newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: BP talks tough on Colombia contract terms.
newsitem.headline: BP talks tough on Colombia contract terms.

text.p: BOGOTA, April 30 Reuter - Officials of British Petroleum Co Plc sent Wednesday one of their strongest signals to date that they could abandon an oil-rich area of eastern Colombia if the government did not sweeten contract terms.

"If you change the recent ministerial resolution we will not earn anything. BP will not work for free on this project and for that reason we must look for a solution," Iain Conn, vice- chairman of BP's Colombian subsidiary BP Exploration, told a congressional hearing.
BP has been involved in protracted wrangling with the state-run oil company Ecopetrol over the terms of its association contract to exploit the Piedemonte block in the eastern plains region.
Under the original sliding-scale contract BP would share an ever-higher proportion of the profits from the field with Ecopetrol in line with rising output.

Conn said Wednesday that if those terms were left in place, BP would make no profit on the $2.1 billion it is currently investing to develop three hydrocarbon formations -- about 15 percent of the total 709,000 acre 297,000 hectare Piedemonte block.

But earlier this month Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar opened the door on a short-term profitability boost when he ruled the contract would take natural gas, not crude, output as the benchmark to determine the cut of the profits that Ecopetrol would take.

In practical terms this would mean BP would take a larger share of the profits for a longer time, thereby carving out a profit margin of about 10 percent on the three formations already discovered -- still well-below the 15 percent margin which BP sees as an international average.

BP has argued that the ministerial resolution regarding the contract is logical given that the largest liquid deposits are not crude but condensates, which were not mentioned in the original contract.

The resolution, however, inflamed nationalist passions among some Colombian lawmakers and leaders of the powerful USO oil workers' union. They argued BP, Colombia's largest single foreign investor, was blackmailing the government with veiled threats to scale back its operations.

But in a session to explain the issues to congressmen, Conn rejected claims that BP was "pressuring or blackmailing" the government, adding, "It is not correct to say the rules of the game cannot be changed if they're to the benefit of everybody. We're talking about the real world of oil production. We're talking about a win-win situation so that we can win together for the good of Colombia."
Speaking to reporters after the session, Villamizar told reporters he was concerned by the prospect of a BP pull-out.
"It worries me a great deal. It would be serious for this country but I hope we can agree some alternative if the resolution is revoked," he said.

The case will now be put to the government's Council of Ministers, comprising president Ernesto Samper and his 15-member cabinet, on May 26. If Villamizar's resolution is revoked the whole contract will be sent back to Ecopetrol's board of directors for further consideration.
Piedemonte is estimated to contain between 500 million and 1 billion barrels of condensates. Commercial production will not begin until the contract wrangle is resolved, Conn said.
